newsitem.title: GERMANY: Expert panel against hasty NATO pullout from Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Expert panel against hasty NATO pullout from Bosnia.

text.p: A group of U.S. and European Balkan specialists said on Thursday a hasty withdrawal by NATO peacekeepers from former Yugoslavia would be disastrous and international forces will be needed for at least two more years.

The International Commission on the Balkans -- an independent panel of European and U.S. politicians, academics and journalists -- said in a report that there was still much instability in the region.

"Outside guarantors, even enforcers of the peace will have to remain in the region -- first and foremost in Bosnia -- for a considerable period," said former Belgian Prime Minister Leo Tindemans, a commission member, in a statement.

The commission was referring to the 52,000-strong NATO-led international peace implementation force (IFOR) deployed in Bosnia whose mandate expires in December. Some NATO members have said this mandate should be extended.

Commission executive director Jacques Rupnik said the military presence should remain in the region at least two more years to ensure the Dayton peace plan's recommendation for a second set of elections within that time.

"We are not talking about an endless international protectorate over the Balkans," Rupnik told Reuters. "But security is the key to the possible emergence of democratic institutions, economic development and future reconciliation."

The seven-member Commission included Simone Veil, former President of the European Parliament, David Anderson, former U.S. ambassador to Yugoslavia and John Roper, former British member of Parliament.
The commission was created in July 1995 under the auspices of the Aspen Institute Berlin and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
